demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is not clinically coherent as a trigger for PTSD centered on the unexpected death of a loved one unless the death involved snakes, which is not indicated. It appears trauma-unrelated and weakly connected to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' implies perceived preventability and personal responsibility during the death event. That can occur, but it is not supported by the rest of the profile, which lacks any memory or trigger content suggesting direct involvement in the loved one's death.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: 'Starting new friendships or relationships' as an avoided strategy is a poor fit for a married 28-year-old male whose trauma is bereavement, and it is not well linked to the stated triggers/appraisals. It suggests interpersonal avoidance without supporting appraisals such as mistrust, fear of loss, or social threat.

vignette: Two years ago, Elias stood in the humid hospital corridor watching the sheets pull up over his younger brother's face. There had been no warning, only a sudden phone call about a car that had crossed the median and struck their mother's old sedan. He had arrived at the scene too late to stop it, too late to pull his brother from the twisted metal. The memory did not arrive as a story so much as a physical weight: the smell of burnt rubber, the sudden silence where laughter had been, and the persistent certainty that he should have protected them and had failed. Since then, Elias had come to believe that the man who used to be a happy person was gone, replaced by someone who was always miserable. The sensation of detachment began quietly, then multiplied. When a dispatcher's voice crackled over his guard radio describing a fatal head-on collision, Elias felt his stomach drop and the fluorescent lights of the correctional facility seem to blur at the edges. He was certain that if he stayed still, the unreality would swallow him whole, so he pressed his palms flat against his face, blocking out the tiered walkways and the distant clamor of inmates. He had learned to steer clear of anything that might tug at the wound. When coworkers gathered in the breakroom to mourn a colleague's daughter, Elias would slip out, refusing to listen, refusing to let the conversation about losing someone anchor him back to that hospital floor. He avoided grief reminders entirely, treating them like live wires that might shock him back into the past. The facility's daily routine offered few respite. During lockdowns, when the heavy steel doors clanged shut and the air grew thick with damp concrete and sweat, Elias would watch the monitors with a stillness that made the other officers glance his way. He did not notice their stares. He noticed only the sudden, unbidden flash of his brother's hands resting too still on the kitchen table, and the way the room would tilt, forcing him to anchor his boots to the floor and wait for the sensation to pass. Over the months, the avoidance calcified into a pattern of restless friction. At home, when his wife, Clara, suggested they drive back to their hometown to visit their parents' graves, Elias found himself manufacturing arguments about finances, about her tone, about anything that could fracture the quiet tension. He picked arguments to drown out the grief, convincing himself that drama was preferable to the suffocating silence where memories lived. The conflicts grew predictable, leaving him exhausted and Clara withdrawn, though he could not bring himself to stop. At work, the weight of his appraisal that he had failed to protect others sat alongside a rigid posture; he grew stiff during counts, scanning the yard with a hyper-focused intensity that left his shoulders permanently knotted and his interactions with inmates clipped and defensive. He had come to believe he had no future, that hope was simply a luxury for people who hadn't witnessed how quickly everything could end. The turning point came during a night shift when a radio bulletin announced another fatal accident on the highway near the facility. The familiar detachment rushed over Elias so fast he had to brace himself against a concrete pillar, hands still pressed to his eyes, breathing shallow until the siren faded. He realized he could no longer pretend the world was safe to navigate. He had come to seek help not because he wanted to forget, but because he was terrified that he would remain a ghost in his own life, permanently untethered from the present. What he hoped for was simply a way to stand in a room without counting exits, to listen to the news without bracing for impact, and to finally believe that he might, in time, be allowed to live again.
